blocks.content: Process versus thread is one of the single most asked operating systems questions in interviews, and it is also one of the most poorly answered. Almost everyone can recite that threads are lighter than processes. Very few can explain why that is true, what it actually costs to create each one, what happens when each one crashes, and when you would deliberately choose one over the other. A genuinely good answer needs all of that, not just the one line.

This chapter builds a precise, memorable distinction between the two, walks through a detailed side by side comparison across memory, creation cost, communication, crash behavior, and context switching, and then applies all of it to a real worked example so the tradeoffs stop being abstract.
1. The One Line Distinction
Before comparing anything in detail, it helps to fix one precise sentence in your head, because most interview follow up questions are really just asking you to expand on it.

blocks.title: The one line to remember
blocks.content: A process is an independent program in execution with its own isolated memory space. A thread is a lightweight unit of execution that lives inside a process and shares that process memory with its sibling threads.

Notice what this sentence already implies. A process is the unit of isolation, it owns its own address space and nothing outside it can read or write that memory without going through the operating system. A thread is the unit of execution inside that boundary, and every thread created inside a given process is, by default, free to read and write the same memory as every other thread in that same process. Everything else in this chapter, the cost of creating them, how they talk to each other, what a crash does, and how expensive it is to switch between them, follows directly from this one fact about memory.

Threads are not simply a cheaper version of a process. They are a different answer to a different question: a process asks how do I isolate this work, a thread asks how do I run this work concurrently while still sharing state.
2. The Side by Side Comparison Table
blocks.text: 2. The Side by Side Comparison Table

blocks.content: This is the table worth memorizing. Every row maps back to the one fact from section one, that a process has its own isolated memory and a thread shares its parent process memory. Read through it once, then read it again while asking yourself why each answer follows from that fact.

All threads of a process read and write the same heap, global variables, and open files."],["Creation cost","Expensive. The operating system must build a brand new memory space, copy or set up page tables, and allocate fresh resources.","Cheap. A thread reuses the parent process memory space, so creation is mostly just allocating a small stack and a thread control block."],["Communication","Requires explicit inter process communication, such as pipes, sockets, shared memory segments, or message queues.","Direct. Since threads already share memory, one thread can simply read or write a shared variable that another thread also sees."],["Crash impact","Isolated. If one process crashes, the operating system tears down only that process, and every other process keeps running.","Can bring down the whole process. Since all threads share memory, a bad pointer or a corrupted shared structure in one thread can corrupt data every other thread in that process depends on."],["Context switch cost","Expensive. Switching to a different process also means switching the full memory mapping, which invalidates cached translations and slows the processor down.","Cheaper. Threads of the same process share the memory mapping, so a switch only needs to swap registers and the stack pointer, not the whole address space."]]}

blocks.title: Read the table as cause and effect
blocks.content: Every row on the process side traces back to isolation, and every row on the thread side traces back to sharing. If you can explain the memory row, you can derive the other four rows from it instead of memorizing them separately.
3. Picturing It: Threads Live Inside a Process
blocks.text: 3. Picturing It: Threads Live Inside a Process

blocks.content: A diagram makes the containment relationship obvious in a way that words alone do not. Two independent processes are drawn as two separate boxes, and inside each box are the threads that belong only to that process.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408309441-122880966.png
blocks.alt: Picturing It: Threads Live Inside a Process

blocks.content: Look closely at what the diagram is saying. Thread 1, Thread 2, and Thread 3 inside process A can all reach into the same memory, so they can pass data between each other simply by writing to a shared variable. But nothing inside process A can reach into process B, and nothing inside process B can reach into process A, not even thread to thread. The dashed line between the two processes is deliberate: there is no direct path, only indirect communication through the operating system if the two processes need to talk at all.
Why this picture explains the whole table
blocks.text: Why this picture explains the whole table

blocks.content: Creation is cheap for a new thread because it is just adding one more box inside an already built process. Creation is expensive for a new process because it means building an entirely new outer box from scratch. A crash inside one thread can corrupt the whole box because the box has no internal walls. A crash inside one process cannot touch the other box because the outer boundary is exactly what the operating system enforces.
4. Worked Example: A Web Server Handling Three Requests
blocks.text: 4. Worked Example: A Web Server Handling Three Requests

blocks.content: Comparisons stay abstract until you apply them to a real system. Consider a web server that needs to handle three requests arriving at the same time, and imagine building it two different ways.
Approach one: a process per request
blocks.text: Approach one: a process per request

blocks.content: The server forks a brand new process for every incoming request. Each of the three processes gets its own full, isolated copy of the server data, its own copy of the connection pool, its own copy of the in memory cache. This is safe: if one request causes that process to crash, the other two processes are completely unaffected and keep serving their users. But it is memory heavy, since three copies of the same cache and connection pool now sit in memory, and it is slow to start, since building a new isolated memory space for every single request is expensive work for the operating system to repeat three times.
Approach two: a thread per request
blocks.text: Approach two: a thread per request

blocks.content: The server instead spins up a lightweight thread for each of the three requests, and all three threads live inside the same single process. They share the same in memory cache and the same connection pool, so no memory is duplicated and no expensive setup is repeated. Threads are cheap to create, so all three can start almost instantly. The tradeoff appears the moment something goes wrong: a bug in the thread handling request one, say a stray write past the end of a shared buffer, could in principle corrupt data that the thread handling request two is reading from that same shared cache, even though request two had nothing to do with the bug.

{"headers":["","Process per request","Thread per request"],"rows":[["Memory use","High, each request duplicates the cache and connection pool","Low, all requests share one cache and one connection pool"],["Startup speed","Slow, a new isolated memory space is built every time","Fast, a thread just reuses the existing process memory space"],["Fault isolation","Strong, one request crashing cannot affect the other two","Weak, one request corrupting shared memory can affect the other two"]]}

blocks.title: There is no universally correct choice here
blocks.content: Real production web servers use both strategies. Some use one process with many worker threads for speed and shared caching. Others use multiple worker processes, sometimes each running its own threads, to get isolation between requests while still getting some of the speed benefit of threads within each worker.
5. When to Prefer One Over the Other
blocks.text: 5. When to Prefer One Over the Other

blocks.content: Once the tradeoffs are clear, the decision of which one to reach for stops being a coin flip and becomes a direct consequence of what the system needs most.

["Prefer processes when strong isolation and fault tolerance matter most, so a crash or bug in one unit of work can never corrupt or take down another unit of work.","Prefer processes when the units of work come from different, possibly untrusted sources, since isolation also acts as a security boundary.","Prefer threads when performance and low overhead matter most, so you need fast creation and fast context switching between many concurrent units of work.","Prefer threads when the units of work genuinely need to share state efficiently, such as a common cache or a common connection pool, and isolation is not the primary concern."]
items: Prefer processes when strong isolation and fault tolerance matter most, so a crash or bug in one unit of work can never corrupt or take down another unit of work.
Prefer processes when the units of work come from different, possibly untrusted sources, since isolation also acts as a security boundary.
Prefer threads when performance and low overhead matter most, so you need fast creation and fast context switching between many concurrent units of work.
Prefer threads when the units of work genuinely need to share state efficiently, such as a common cache or a common connection pool, and isolation is not the primary concern.

blocks.content: A useful shortcut is to ask what a crash should be allowed to do. If a crash in one unit of work must never be allowed to affect another, reach for processes. If the units of work are trusted, cooperating parts of the same task and sharing data between them is the whole point, reach for threads.
6. Common Mistakes in Interview Answers

This topic is asked constantly precisely because it is easy to answer shallowly. Interviewers can tell within a sentence or two whether a candidate actually understands the mechanism or is repeating a phrase they memorized.

["Saying only that threads are lighter than processes, without being able to explain why, which comes down to memory sharing versus memory isolation.","Not being able to explain the tradeoff a crash implies for each: a process crash is contained, a thread crash risks corrupting the whole process because every thread in it shares the same memory.","Forgetting that communication is a direct consequence of the memory model, so processes need explicit inter process communication while threads can just share a variable.","Treating threads as strictly better because they are cheaper, without acknowledging that cheapness comes at the direct cost of losing isolation.","Being unable to give a concrete example, such as the web server case, when asked to justify a choice between the two in a real system."]
items: Saying only that threads are lighter than processes, without being able to explain why, which comes down to memory sharing versus memory isolation.
Not being able to explain the tradeoff a crash implies for each: a process crash is contained, a thread crash risks corrupting the whole process because every thread in it shares the same memory.
Forgetting that communication is a direct consequence of the memory model, so processes need explicit inter process communication while threads can just share a variable.
Treating threads as strictly better because they are cheaper, without acknowledging that cheapness comes at the direct cost of losing isolation.
Being unable to give a concrete example, such as the web server case, when asked to justify a choice between the two in a real system.

blocks.title: The fix is always the same
blocks.content: Anchor every answer back to the one line from section one. Isolation versus sharing explains creation cost, communication, crash impact, and context switch cost, all at once, and it is the difference between reciting facts and demonstrating understanding.
7. Closing: Why This Table Is Worth Memorizing
blocks.text: 7. Closing: Why This Table Is Worth Memorizing

blocks.content: Process versus thread keeps coming up because it sits underneath so much of the rest of operating systems and system design: how a web server scales, how a database engine isolates connections, why one crashing microservice does not take down its neighbors, why a browser tab crashing does not close every other tab. The comparison table in section two is small enough to hold in your head and general enough to explain all of those situations.

Being able to recite that table from memory, and more importantly being able to explain why each row follows from the memory model in section one, is exactly what separates a candidate who memorized a definition from one who understands the tradeoff. That is the bar this chapter aims to get you past.
